Generally, I don't do individual reviews on the comments on a Public Comment post, unless the comment contains an error that I find egregious. But, this comment requires a disclaimer, as I am the author of the 'Articles' & 'Scientific Results' sections of the VentureBeat article, and Administrative Director of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Next, I think that sigma's answer, while not ideal, is not terrible (at least from the point of view of a mathematician - it is designed to be easy to understand while teasing out the key issues). Unfortunately, none of the respondents on this question have a sufficient "N", so they can't really be critiqued. That said, two comments stand out. One is that the commenters don't seem to be applying the Fermi approach that the commenter above is suggesting (and which I'm not suggesting, either). Instead, they seem to be suggesting that they apply their nationwide estimate, which is not a good way to come up with a probability. In order to make such an estimate, you would need data on the probabilities that top countries have of solving each of the problems. And those probabilities change over time, as new techniques are developed and old ones fail. And they differ drastically for each problem - indeed, that is one of the huge difficulties in attacking these problems. Another comment is that, as a mathematician, I would say that the Hodge Conjecture is not nearly as important to mathematicians as the Riemann Hypothesis. Indeed, I would argue that its solution would be no less significant than that of the Riemann Hypothesis, or, for that matter, the solution of the Poincaré Problem. And if human beings do solve it, it will be quite a historic feat - at the very least as big as the solution of the Poincaré Conjecture, and very likely much larger. The Hodge Conjecture touches on some of the deepest and most important issues in mathematics - indeed, some of the deepest and most important issues in all of human knowledge. A solution of the conjecture will literally change human understanding of the subject - of geometry, for one - in monumental ways. Additionally, it is currently regarded as one of the hardest unsolved problems in mathematics - i.e., one of the hardest open problems. The only significant issue that the Hodge Conjecture has not quite yet accomplished is to make it into a 'List of Millennium Problems'. Finally, let me say that I am surprised that no one has mentioned the fact that the Hodge Conjecture is already 'classified solve', by Jørgen Pedersen, in 2011.
